lesson_title: The Supplier Says You Owe More: Reconciliations
hook_text: Their statement says R48 700. Your book says R29 100. Skip the check and you pay R13 400 too much.
clip_script: Month-end. Makoya Wholesalers sends a statement: you owe forty-eight thousand seven hundred. Your own book says twenty-nine thousand one hundred. Before anyone shouts — sit down and take the differences one by one, because each belongs to somebody. Their statement has an invoice for six thousand two hundred: the goods really arrived on the twenty-ninth, so YOUR book is behind — it catches up. You paid eight thousand four hundred on the twenty-eighth; their statement was printed on the twenty-fifth — their side comes down. The nine-fifty discount they promised isn't processed yet — down again. The damaged goods you returned — down again. And then the gem: an invoice for two thousand seven hundred and fifty that is not yours at all. Somebody at Makoya posted another customer's shopping to YOUR account. Down once more. Now both records say the same thing: thirty-five thousand three hundred. THAT is what you pay. Count what twenty minutes of checking was worth: pay the raw statement and you throw away thirteen thousand four hundred rand — including someone else's groceries. And here is the dangerous part: fake invoices flow toward businesses that never check, because word gets around about who pays blind. So the rule is one sentence long. Never pay a statement. Pay a RECONCILED statement.
visual_style: Two paper columns facing each other like duelling receipts, line items sliding down or across as each difference finds its owner; the wrong-customer invoice glowing red before it drops; both columns clicking to the same total.
pacing: Confrontational open, rhythmic item-by-item beats, slow reveal on the stranger's invoice, punchy one-line rule to close.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and reconcile any statement, bank account or debtors' book the paper sets.
